why: Testing where a pebble sits, what soap does and how salt changes floating helps your child explain why a boat stays upright and rides high.
teaser: Float a paper boat down the curb, then tip it with a pebble, power it with soap, read a ship's load lines and meet a ship made of concrete.
title: The Hidden Tricks of a Paper Boat
question: What keeps a paper boat upright, and what can make it go?
idea: Weight kept low and centered keeps a boat steady. Water has a stretchy skin, and soap behind a boat lets the skin in front pull it forward. Salty water pushes up harder, so boats ride higher in it, and a hollow shape lets even concrete float.

curiosity.intro: Start with a paper boat on a rain stream. Then tip it with a pebble, power it with soap, read a ship's load lines and meet a ship made of concrete.
curiosity.carryForward: Next time you float a boat, guess where its weight should go before you load it.

questions.question: Why does a pebble on the rim tip the boat?
questions.notice: Compare the level boat, with its pebble low in the middle, and the leaning boat, with its pebble on the rim.
questions.say: Weight that sits low and in the middle keeps a boat steady. Weight up high or out at the edge pulls that side down, so the boat tips. Big ships carry heavy ballast, like water or rocks, deep in their bottoms so they stay upright in waves.
questions.try: Fold two paper boats and float them in a sink. Put a coin low in the middle of one and on the rim of the other. Which one stays level?

questions.question: How can soap push a boat?
questions.notice: Find the tiny soap drop at the back of the boat, the rainbow film spreading behind it and the pepper flakes pushed to the edge.
questions.say: The top of water pulls together like a stretchy skin. That pull is called surface tension. Soap weakens the skin wherever it lands. The skin in front of the boat is still strong, so it pulls the boat forward, like a tug-of-war where one side lets go.
questions.try: Cut a small boat shape from card with a notch at the back. Float it in a tray of water, then touch a drop of dish soap into the notch. Change the water before you try again.

questions.question: Why do ships have lines painted on their sides?
questions.notice: Find the circle with a bar through it and the ladder of short stripes just above the water.
questions.say: Those marks are load lines. Salty sea water is heavier than fresh river water, so it pushes up harder and a ship floats higher in it. Sailors load cargo only until the right line reaches the water, so the ship stays safe in salty, fresh or stormy winter seas.
questions.try: Next time you see a big boat, look near the water. Can you find a circle and some stripes?

questions.question: How can a ship made of concrete float?
questions.notice: Find the rough grey concrete hull, its rust streaks, and the line where it meets the calm harbour water.
questions.say: A solid block of concrete sinks. A ship shape is different: its walls wrap around a lot of air. The hollow hull pushes aside so much water that the water pushes back up hard enough to hold it. People built concrete ships long ago, and some still float as harbour walls.
questions.try: Roll a ball of clay and drop it in water. Then press the same clay into a little bowl shape and float it. What changed?

plates.title: A boat on the curb
plates.alt: On a wet sidewalk after rain, Big Wonderer crouches low and Little Wonderer kneels beside it, one mitten reaching toward a shallow stream along the curb. A small white folded paper boat floats upright on the stream among fallen yellow leaves.
plates.caption: A paper boat rides the rain stream and stays upright. Why doesn't it tip, and could it move with no wind?

plates.title: Low and steady
plates.alt: Two white paper boats float in a round stone basin. The left boat has a grey pebble low in its middle and sits level; the right boat has the same kind of pebble up on its rim and leans to that side.
plates.caption: Pebble low in the middle: the boat floats level. Pebble on the rim: the boat leans. Ships carry heavy ballast down low.

plates.title: A soap motor
plates.alt: A white paper boat floats in a wide shallow tray of water sprinkled with pepper flakes. Behind the boat a tiny clear drop of soap spreads a rainbow film, and the pepper flakes have been pushed back toward the tray's rim.
plates.caption: Soap weakens the water's stretchy skin behind the boat. The stronger skin in front pulls, and the boat glides forward.

plates.title: Lines on a ship
plates.alt: The dark, rust-streaked hull of a big ship moored in a harbour. Painted on its side just above the water is a white circle with a bar through it and a short ladder of white stripes. A paper boat floats nearby beside the dock.
plates.caption: Load lines, or Plimsoll marks, show how deep a loaded ship may safely sit in fresh, salty or winter water.

plates.title: A salty test
plates.alt: Indoors beside a sunny window, Big Wonderer kneels and points while Little Wonderer sits forward on a cushion. On a low table sit two clear bowls of water, each with a paper boat; the boat in the right bowl rides higher, and a small dish of salt sits beside it.
plates.caption: Same boat, same pebble, but the salty bowl lifts it higher. Floating depends on the water, too.

plates.title: A ship of stone
plates.alt: An old grey concrete ship with rust streaks and small plants growing along its rail floats moored by thick ropes beside a harbour wall at sunset, with a small lighthouse in the distance.

tasks.worked: 6300 ÷ 9 = 700. Each row gets the same number.

tasks.prompt: The big one stirs 1150 grains of salt into each of 7 bowls. How many grains is that?
tasks.hint: Think 1000 × 7 and 150 × 7, then add.

tasks.prompt: In a pretend count, 7200 boats float in salty water and 3845 float in fresh water. How many more float in salty water?
tasks.hint: Regroup, then subtract each place.

tasks.prompt: Workers pour 2500 kilograms of concrete for each of 3 hull walls. How many kilograms is that?
There are 8100 rivets shared equally among 10 sections of a hull. How many rivets are in each section?
tasks.hint: Think which number times 10 makes 8100.
tasks.worked: 8100 ÷ 10 = 810. Each section gets the same number.

quiz.title: Four looks at a paper boat
quiz.intro: Follow the boat from a rain stream to a ship made of concrete.

questions.prompt: Where should a pebble go for a steady boat?
questions.answer: Weight low and in the middle keeps a boat steady.

questions.prompt: What does soap do to the water's skin?
questions.answer: Soap weakens the skin behind the boat, so the skin in front pulls it forward.

questions.prompt: Why paint load lines on a ship?
questions.answer: The lines show how much cargo is safe in each kind of water.

questions.prompt: Which water lifts a boat higher?
questions.answer: Salty water pushes up harder, so the boat rides higher.

titleCard.title: The Hidden Tricks of a Paper Boat
titleCard.line: A pebble, a drop of soap, a pinch of salt, and a ship made of stone.

poem.title: Upper Deck, Please
lines: A pebble demanded a seat on the rim.
The boat dipped its edge. They both went for a swim.
Little Wonderer fished out the wreck.
“Let's find you a cabin below the top deck.”
Big Wonderer moved it. The boat floated flat,
with weight in the middle, down low where it sat.
The pebble requested the top deck instead.
They gave it a snorkel to wear on its head.

drawing.alt: Black-ink line drawing: Big Wonderer leans in while Little Wonderer steps toward a low basin of water, holding up a small pebble in one mitten. In the basin a paper boat floats level with a pebble sitting low in its middle.
